arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Justice Thomas asked the government's lawyer what the Court should do if it finds itself in equipoise on the question.

Justice Kavanaugh noted Congress often drafts overlapping language and ordinary people communicate redundantly, preferring overlap over leaving a hole. He also questioned how courts can tell when drafters repeat themselves, citing competing legal authorities on the point.

the opposing side's lawyer argued the government's factual showing fell short, saying a week is probably not long enough under the relevant standard. And That this is not just allegations because it goes to jurisdiction.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: The Federal Tort Claims Act generally lets people sue the government for harm caused by federal employees. But it carves out a postal exception preserving US immunity for claims arising out of the loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission of mail. The case turns on how far that exception reaches.

sections.heading: How the case got here
paragraphs: A the opposing side alleges her mail never reached its destination because postal employees intentionally withheld it and returned it to sender. The government argues the postal exception bars such claims. The case reached the Supreme Court after lower-court proceedings.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: The Postal Service wants the Court to hold that the postal exception preserves its immunity, so the claim cannot proceed. It argues dictionary definitions and pre-FTCA cases show miscarriage broadly covered any time mail failed to arrive.

the opposing side wants her suit to proceed. Her lawyer argued no ordinary speaker would say the mail carrier lost her mail when employees intentionally withheld it. And Pointed to a differently worded statute about government employees causing loss.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: The government's lawyer argued the exception covers intentional withholding because miscarriage had a broad ordinary meaning encompassing any failure of mail to arrive.
the opposing side's lawyer argued the government never disputed that ordinary speakers would not call intentionally withheld mail lost, and distinguished a separate statute worded differently.

sections.heading: What the Court decided
paragraphs: The Federal Tort Claims Act's postal exception covers harm from mail that is intentionally not delivered, so the United States keeps sovereign immunity over such claims. Both miscarriage and loss of mail can result from a Postal Service's deliberate failure to deliver it.
The Supreme Court vacated the Fifth Circuit's judgment and remanded the case for further proceedings.
